chunks: "A CSA is basically an op-amp configured as a difference amplifier, but optimized and packaged for measuring a shunt. The differences are what matter. First, resistor matching.
With a regular op-amp I build the gain with discrete resistors, and 0. 1 percent parts only give about 80 decibels CMRR at a gain of 50.
A CSA has the resistors on-die, trimmed to a few ppm of matching, so CMRR is typically 100 to 120 decibels and the gain is accurate to within a percent or better with low drift.
Second, common-mode range. A regular op-amp's inputs have to stay within its supply, so it can't read a shunt on a 48 volt bus if it's powered from 5 volts.
Many CSAs are designed so the inputs can sit far above, even well outside, their supply.
Third, offset: CSAs often have zero-drift architectures with a few microvolts, whereas a general-purpose op-amp may have millivolts, which sets the minimum current I can measure.
CSAs also integrate protection, REF pins for bidirectional operation, and sometimes comparators, and they save board area and design time.
The op-amp wins on flexibility, cost at very low volume, and when the bus is within the supply and I can accept moderate accuracy."
